{"markdown":"# Issues Memo — Master Services Agreement (Brightline)

**To:** Deal team 
**From:** In-house counsel 
**Re:** Playbook review of the Master Services Agreement — verified findings 
**Privileged & confidential / attorney work product**

---

## 1. Executive summary

We have completed our playbook review of the Master Services Agreement. The document is, on the whole, unusually favourable to us: 16 of the 18 rules reviewed sit at our **preferred** position, and several run better than preferred (Vendor-granted MFN in § 7.6, Vendor non-compete in § 12.4, express confirmation in § 12.3 that we have given no exclusivity, non-compete, MFN, minimum-volume or no-hire commitment). Ownership of Deliverables and Customer Data (§ 14), the Vendor indemnity (§ 20), transition assistance and data return (§ 11), audit rights (§ 22), assignment and change of control (§ 24), and governing law and venue (§ 28) all require no redline.

Two items require action, both critical and both concerning money:

1. **§ 7.7 — Customer-payable liquidated damages.** A ten-day payment delay triggers 15% of annual Fees *per week*. This compounds past the remaining contract value within weeks off a minor breach. This is walk-away territory and far outside our fallback (a single early-termination fee capped at three months' Fees).
2. **§ 21.1 — illusory liability cap.** The cap keys to "Fees", which § 1.5 defines as only the Implementation Fee, and § 1.6 fixes that at a one-time USD 12,000 charge under the first Order Form. The twelve-month look-back therefore captures nothing recurring, even though recurring spend plainly exists (§ 7.2 annual subscription Fees invoiced in advance; § 8.3 increases to recurring Fees). The effective ceiling on Vendor's exposure is USD 12,000 — below the six-months'-fees walk-away floor — while our payment obligations sit outside the cap under § 21.3.

Notably, the structural elements of § 21 are already strong (express mutuality, mutual consequential-damages exclusion, and a full set of uncapped Excluded Claims covering confidentiality, data protection and security, indemnification, gross negligence, wilful misconduct, fraud and IP infringement). The defect is confined to the cap quantum, so our proposed fix is a single targeted amendment.

---

## 2. Findings table

| Severity | Rule | Status | Section | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Critical | LD — Liquidated damages and penalties payable by Customer | **Deviation** | § 7.7 (FEES, INVOICING, AND TAXES) | 15% of annual Fees per week after a 10-day delay; walk-away territory |
| Critical | LOL-CAP — Limitation of liability: cap, mutuality and carve-outs | **Deviation** | § 21 (LIMITATION OF LIABILITY) | Cap keys to a one-time USD 12,000 Implementation Fee; fails the 12-months'-fees fallback |
| Critical | INDEMN — Indemnification by Vendor | Compliant | § 20 (INDEMNIFICATION) | Preferred in full; indemnity uncapped via § 21.3 Excluded Claims |
| Critical | IP — Ownership of deliverables and Customer Data | Compliant | § 14 (INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY AND DELIVERABLES) | Present assignment of Deliverables; we own Customer Data; perpetual § 13.2 licence |
| High | ASSIGN — Assignment and change of control | Compliant | § 24 (ASSIGNMENT AND CHANGE OF CONTROL) | Free Affiliate/successor assignment for us; § 24.4 bars repricing on our change of control |
| High | EXCLUSIVITY — Exclusivity obligations binding Customer | Compliant | § 12 (CUSTOMER RESPONSIBILITIES) | § 12.3 affirmative disclaimer; § 2.1 no minimum commitment |
| High | LICENSE — Licence grant scope | Compliant | § 13 (ACCESS RIGHTS AND LICENCE) | Extends to Affiliates and contractors; § 13.3 revocation narrower than preferred |
| High | NONCOMPETE — Non-compete restrictions on Customer | Compliant | § 12 (CUSTOMER RESPONSIBILITIES) | No field-of-use or post-term covenant on us; § 12.4 runs in our favour |
| High | T4C — Termination for convenience | Compliant | § 9 (TERMINATION) | § 9.4 right for us; 30 days' notice via § 29.4; prepaid Fees refunded |
| Medium | AUDIT — Audit rights against Customer | Compliant | § 22 (AUDIT RIGHTS) | Once per 12 months, 30 days' notice, no direct system access |
| Medium | GOVLAW — Governing law and venue | Compliant | § 28 (GOVERNING LAW AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION) | New York law and exclusive New York County courts; no arbitration |
| Medium | MFN — Most-favoured-nation obligations burdening Customer | Compliant | § 7 (FEES, INVOICING, AND TAXES) | § 7.6 MFN runs in our favour; retain |
| Medium | MINCOMMIT — Minimum purchase commitments and volume restrictions | Compliant | § 2 (AGREEMENT STRUCTURE AND SCOPE) | § 2.1 no minimum quantity; non-order is not a shortfall |
| Medium | NOSOLICIT — Non-solicitation of employees binding Customer | Compliant | § 12 (CUSTOMER RESPONSIBILITIES) | § 12.3 preserves general-recruitment hiring; no no-hire covenant |
| Medium | RENEWAL — Auto-renewal and non-renewal notice window | Compliant | § 8 (TERM AND RENEWAL) | 12-month renewals, 30-day opt-out, uplift capped at lesser of CPI-U and 3% |
| Medium | TRANSITION — Post-termination transition assistance and data return | Compliant | § 11 (TRANSITION ASSISTANCE AND DATA RETURN) | Up to 6 months' assistance; 30-day machine-readable return; certified deletion |
| Medium | WARRANTY — Performance warranty and duration | Compliant | § 19 (WARRANTIES) | Hosted software warranted throughout the term; § 19.5 disclaimer does not cut back express warranties |
| Low | INSURANCE — Vendor insurance | Compliant | § 18 (INSURANCE) | CGL, workers' comp, E&O USD 2M, cyber USD 5M, plus certificates on request |

All findings above carry a **pass** verification status.

---

## 3. Walk-away items

Two findings sit in walk-away territory as our playbook defines it. Neither should be conceded without escalation to the business owner.

**(a) § 7.7 — liquidated damages for late payment.** Fifteen percent of annual Fees per week, triggered by a ten-day delay, compounds past the remaining contract value within weeks and is triggered by a minor breach. Our fallback tolerates at most a single early-termination fee capped at three months' Fees; this is an order of magnitude beyond that. We note that no other Customer-payable liquidated amount exists in the document — § 9.4 limits us to accrued Fees on convenience termination, § 2.1 disclaims minimum commitments, § 27 permits termination without penalty, and the § 22.2 audit shortfall is a true-up of amounts owed rather than a liquidated sum — so § 7.7 is the sole exposure and can be excised cleanly. Vendor retains its ordinary non-payment remedies, including termination for material breach under § 9.1.

**(b) § 21.1 — effective cap of USD 12,000.** Because "Fees" is defined as the one-time Implementation Fee (§§ 1.5, 1.6) and the cap is further confined to the first Order Form, the twelve-month look-back captures no recurring spend. The resulting ceiling falls far below six months' fees, which our playbook treats as walk-away. The asymmetry is compounded by § 21.3, which places our payment obligations outside the cap.

---

## 4. Proposed positions on the two deviations

**§ 7.7 — LD.** Replace the Customer-payable liquidated damages with an express statement that Customer owes no liquidated damages or penalties. This is our preferred position; Vendor's non-payment remedies under § 9.1 are unaffected.

> [Playbook] We have removed the late-payment liquidated damages and confirmed that no liquidated damages or penalties are payable by Customer. At 15% of annual Fees per week from a ten-day delay, the charge compounds past the remaining contract value and is triggered by a minor breach, which is outside our position even at fallback (a single early-termination fee capped at three months' Fees). Vendor retains its ordinary remedies for non-payment, including termination for material breach under § 9.1.

**§ 21.1 — LOL-CAP.** Substitute the narrow "Fees … under the first Order Form" basis with all amounts paid or payable under the Agreement in the preceding twelve months, subject to a USD 1,000,000 floor. We deliberately did **not** broaden the § 1.5 "Fees" definition, since that would also inflate our own liquidated-damages exposure under § 7.7; the fix is contained within the liability section. Mutuality, the § 21.2 consequential-damages exclusion and the § 21.3 Excluded Claims are preserved untouched.

> [Playbook] We have amended the cap to the greater of all amounts paid or payable under the Agreement in the twelve months preceding the claim and USD 1,000,000. As drafted, the cap keys to "Fees", which § 1.5 limits to the one-time USD 12,000 Implementation Fee under the first Order Form, so the twelve-month look-back captures no recurring spend and the effective ceiling sits well below our floor of twelve months' fees. We have left the § 1.5 definition, the mutuality language, § 21.2 and the § 21.3 Excluded Claims unchanged.

---

## 5. Next steps

1. **Issue the two redlines** (§ 7.7 deletion and § 21.1 cap substitution) as our only substantive changes, and say so expressly to Vendor — a two-issue markup on an eighteen-rule review should close quickly.
2. **Confirm the recurring-fee run-rate** with the business owner so we can pressure-test the USD 1,000,000 floor against twelve months of actual subscription spend and, if the run-rate is materially higher, hold for the greater-of formulation as drafted.
3. **Escalate before conceding** on either item: both sit in walk-away territory, and § 21.1 in particular caps Vendor's exposure at USD 12,000 while our payment obligations remain uncapped under § 21.3.
4. **Police individual Order Forms.** Under § 2.2 an Order Form may vary a provision it expressly identifies. We should screen each Order Form for a longer non-renewal notice window or a larger uplift than § 8.3 permits, and for any importation of audit or exclusivity terms (§ 2.3 already blocks website, click-through, portal and invoice terms).
5. **Retain the counterparty-favourable-to-us terms** without comment: the § 7.6 MFN, the § 12.4 Vendor non-compete, the § 12.3 disclaimers, the § 13.3 narrowed revocation trigger, the § 11.1 rate protection on transition assistance, and the unconditional § 18.1 cyber limit.
6. **Diligence note only** (no redline sought): the § 19.3 malicious-code warranty is qualified to code intentionally introduced by Vendor, and Deliverable conformance runs 90 days rather than 12 months; the § 8.1 three-year initial term is a commercial point for the business owner rather than a playbook issue.

*This memo reflects only the verified findings supplied and the sections cited within them.*"}
